gaps_and_pitfalls.issue: Printed (22.9) has weight e^{a omega}; the integral diverges unless the weight is e^{-a omega} (a > 0). The closed form on the right is correct for e^{-a omega}, which we checked numerically.
gaps_and_pitfalls.impact_on_learner: A careful reader cannot reproduce the closed form and may doubt the result.
gaps_and_pitfalls.suggestion: Use e^{-a omega} and derive via the Laplace transform of J0: integral of e^{-s omega} J0(omega rho) = (s^2 + rho^2)^{-1/2} with s = a -/+ it.

gaps_and_pitfalls.issue: In the printed gamma for the Weber-Wheeler pulse the last bracket contains (a^2 + rho^2) instead of (a^2 + rho^2)^2; only the squared version is dimensionally consistent and satisfies (22.6)-(22.7) (we verified numerically).
gaps_and_pitfalls.impact_on_learner: Anyone checking gamma against the field equations gets a mismatch.
gaps_and_pitfalls.suggestion: Teach the corrected formula and point out that the bracket is |(a - it)^2 + rho^2|^2.

gaps_and_pitfalls.impact_on_learner: Makes the original paper hard to look up and obscures the link to Weber's detector work.
gaps_and_pitfalls.suggestion: Cite Weber and Wheeler, Reviews of Modern Physics (1957).

gaps_and_pitfalls.issue: The text says the impulsive wave is like the plane wave of Fig. 22.1 except with a single front, then cites Fig. 22.1 again; the first reference presumably intended the linearized plane-wave figure of Chapter 21.
gaps_and_pitfalls.impact_on_learner: Circular figure reference confuses what is being compared.
gaps_and_pitfalls.suggestion: Show the oscillatory linear plane wave (DIV Fig. 21.1) beside the impulsive one.

gaps_and_pitfalls.issue: The Penrose-Khan discussion says an observer near the caustic in region II will be swept into region III. Along future-directed causal curves u and v cannot decrease, so from region II (u > 0) one can only enter region IV.
gaps_and_pitfalls.impact_on_learner: Contradicts the causal structure the diagram is meant to teach.
gaps_and_pitfalls.suggestion: Read 'region III' as 'region IV' and demonstrate with the monotonicity of u and v along timelike curves.

gaps_and_pitfalls.issue: Exercise 22.5 writes g-bar as a function of v-bar; for a plane wave in Rosen form both transverse functions depend on the same null coordinate u-bar.
gaps_and_pitfalls.impact_on_learner: Learners may think the alternative convention allows v dependence and fail to match (22.10).
gaps_and_pitfalls.suggestion: Correct the argument to u-bar before assigning the exercise.

gaps_and_pitfalls.issue: The step from surface-forming orbits to [V, W] = 0 is terse: Frobenius only puts the bracket in the span of V and W, and commutation relies on the abelian nature of the chosen symmetry groups.
gaps_and_pitfalls.impact_on_learner: Readers may believe any two Killing vectors with 2-surface orbits commute.
gaps_and_pitfalls.suggestion: Note the counterexample of rotations on a sphere (orbits are surfaces but generators do not commute) and state commutation as part of the assumption.

gaps_and_pitfalls.issue: The Einstein-Rosen reduction silently uses two facts it never states. First, the area radius (CD)^{1/2} can serve as a coordinate only if its gradient is spacelike (not automatic in cosmological settings). Second, after passing to conformal coordinates (t', rho') the primes are dropped as though rho' were still the area radius; that is legitimate only because the vacuum equations make (CD)^{1/2} a solution of the flat 2D wave equation in the (t, rho) block, so it can be taken as one conformal coordinate with its harmonic conjugate as time.
gaps_and_pitfalls.impact_on_learner: A careful reader sees two coordinate choices (area radius and conformal gauge) that appear to use up more freedom than a 2-metric has, and cannot justify the final form (22.4).
gaps_and_pitfalls.suggestion: Before quoting (22.4), show that a combination of the vacuum equations makes sqrt(CD) a solution of the 2D wave equation of the (t, rho) block. In null coordinates it then splits as F(v) + G(u), so F + G and F - G can be used as new rho and t, which keeps the block conformally flat. State the spacelike-gradient assumption explicitly.

gaps_and_pitfalls.issue: The Einstein-Rosen field equations (22.5)-(22.7) are quoted without derivation, and axis regularity (gamma = 0 on the axis to avoid a conical singularity) and the physical meaning of gamma (C-energy) are not discussed.
gaps_and_pitfalls.impact_on_learner: gamma appears as an auxiliary function with no geometric meaning; the energy claim of Weber and Wheeler is unsupported.
gaps_and_pitfalls.suggestion: Add a short computation (or symbolic-algebra notebook) and explain that the large-radius value of gamma measures a deficit angle related to energy per unit length.

gaps_and_pitfalls.issue: The statement that the waves lose planar symmetry after impact is loose: d/dy and d/dz remain Killing vectors in region IV.
gaps_and_pitfalls.impact_on_learner: Conflicts with the Szekeres assumption two paragraphs later that both Killing vectors exist everywhere.
gaps_and_pitfalls.suggestion: Say instead that the scattered waves are no longer pure plane (null, type N) waves; link to the Petrov classification in Chapter 23.

gaps_and_pitfalls.issue: No amplitude parameter appears in f = 1 + u theta(u); the Penrose-Khan coordinates are silently normalized so each wave has unit focal length, which also fixes the positions of the caustics and singularity.
gaps_and_pitfalls.impact_on_learner: Learners may think u = 1 and u^2 + v^2 = 1 are universal rather than set by wave strength.
gaps_and_pitfalls.suggestion: Reintroduce strengths via f = 1 + u theta/a, g = 1 - u theta/a and show the diagram scaling.

gaps_and_pitfalls.issue: The physical effect of a plane wave on free particles is only gestured at (transverse acceleration in a sandwich wave); no geodesic or geodesic-deviation equation is written for the exact wave.
gaps_and_pitfalls.impact_on_learner: The focusing that drives the whole Penrose-Khan story is never shown quantitatively.
gaps_and_pitfalls.suggestion: Derive the Brinkmann transverse equations Y'' = hY, Z'' = -hZ and apply them to h = delta.

gaps_and_pitfalls.issue: Rosen coordinates generically break down where f or g vanish even for smooth waves; the text mentions fold singularities only in the collision context.
gaps_and_pitfalls.impact_on_learner: Misreading metric-function zeros as physical singularities.
gaps_and_pitfalls.suggestion: Emphasize that Brinkmann coordinates are global for plane waves and that Rosen coordinates follow a focusing congruence.

gaps_and_pitfalls.issue: Heavy symbol reuse: V, W as Killing vectors; U, V as Brinkmann coordinates; U, V, W, M as Szekeres metric functions; rho as radius and as density; C as function and constant.
gaps_and_pitfalls.impact_on_learner: Easy to conflate objects when moving between sections.
gaps_and_pitfalls.suggestion: Use distinct symbols in app and tutor materials (e.g. xi, eta for Killing vectors).

gaps_and_pitfalls.issue: Section 22.6 presents singularity formation as the generic outcome, reflecting the 1970s view. Later work (for example Chandrasekhar and Xanthopoulos in the mid-1980s) found colliding-wave solutions with Killing-Cauchy horizons instead, subsequently argued to be unstable.
gaps_and_pitfalls.impact_on_learner: An oversimplified picture of the literature.
gaps_and_pitfalls.suggestion: Mention the horizon-forming solutions and their instability, pointing to Griffiths (1991).

gaps_and_pitfalls.issue: The avoidability of timelike and unavoidability of spacelike singularities is asserted without argument.
gaps_and_pitfalls.impact_on_learner: Readers without the black-hole chapters take it on faith.
gaps_and_pitfalls.suggestion: Show on the Penrose-Khan diagram that the arc u^2 + v^2 = 1 lies in the future of every point in region IV.

tutor_notes: Open with: 'Chapter 21 treated waves as tiny ripples that pass through each other. What might change if the ripples are not tiny?' Then ask why a pulsating spherical star cannot radiate (Birkhoff).

Order of explanation: symmetry ladder, Einstein-Rosen (linear core), Rosen plane waves (one ODE), Brinkmann form (superposition), impulsive wave (distributions), Penrose-Khan diagram, Szekeres framework.
Before 22.2, check the learner is comfortable with Killing vectors as symmetries and with conformal flatness in 2D; before 22.4, with the delta as a distribution.
When presenting (22.9) and the gamma formula, use the corrected versions (e^{-a omega}; (a^2 + rho^2)^2) and tell the learner the book has misprints so they do not lose confidence.
Check understanding: 'Where is the curvature of an impulsive wave, and what is Ricci there?' Expected: only on u = 0, delta-like Riemann, Ricci zero everywhere.

Build physical intuition with the lens picture: after an impulsive wave, y-separations grow and z-separations shrink linearly, meeting at u = 1. Then reveal that Penrose-Khan region II is exactly this and that u = 1 is the caustic.
Check understanding: 'Which of u = 1 and u^2 + v^2 = 1 is a real singularity, and how would you tell?' Expected: the latter, because curvature invariants diverge.

If the learner asks why co-moving waves superpose but colliding ones do not: point to the Brinkmann metric being linear in h and the absence of any cross-coupling when both profiles depend on the same U.

If the learner asks whether this is relevant to LIGO: plane waves are excellent local models far from sources, but amplitudes are about 1e-21, far too weak for collision singularities to matter astrophysically.
Fix the causal slip on p. 458: from region II an observer can only move into region IV, not III; use it as an exercise in reading null coordinates.
Common question: 'Do the waves lose their symmetry after the collision?' Answer: the two translational Killing vectors survive; the waves stop being pure plane waves.
For advanced learners, connect the collision singularity to focusing (Raychaudhuri-type arguments) and to the characteristic initial value problem of Chapter 23.
Keep symbols distinct when speaking: say 'Brinkmann U' versus 'Szekeres function U', and 'radius rho' versus 'density rho'.
